words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as hǎo de. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 好的，我知道了. Hindari: 好的 means you agree or understand — if you cannot do it yet, say what blocks you.
words.when: Remember 好的 like the word you’ll use when you safely acknowledge an instruction or agreement in chat or an office talk — neutral, ready to follow through.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use it as a default workplace yes in WeChat/email and face-to-face: you heard the ask and you’ll act. Pair often with 我知道了. It does not by itself excuse a missed deadline — if you cannot deliver, explain the constraint instead of empty 好的.

example.zh: 好的，我下午把文件发给你。
example.pinyin: Hǎo de, wǒ xiàwǔ bǎ wénjiàn fā gěi nǐ.
example.en: Okay — I’ll send you the file this afternoon.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as xíng. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 行，就这样. Hindari: do not read this sense as háng; for “okay,” the reading is xíng. With a new boss, 好的 is usually safer than casual 行.
words.when: Remember 行 like the word you’ll use when a proposal already suits you and you want a short, spoken yes — then lock it with 就这样.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use spoken 行 for casual agreement among peers: the plan works, move on. It is lighter and less formal than 好的; toward a new manager, prefer 好的. Never confuse the “okay” reading xíng with the surname/line-of-business reading háng.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as kěyǐ. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 可以安排. Hindari: 可以 marks permission or that a plan is possible; personal ability is often better as 能.
words.when: Remember 可以 like the word you’ll use when you grant permission or say a plan is workable — a notch more neutral than casual 行.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 可以 for “that’s fine / we can do that / it’s allowed,” often before a soft next step (我先看一下, 可以安排). For “I am able to,” 能 is often clearer. In office replies it softens yes without the buddy tone of 行.

example.en: That’s fine — let me take a look first.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as méi wèntí. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 没问题，我来处理. Hindari: do not promise 没问题 if the deadline or details are still unclear.
words.when: Remember 没问题 like the word you’ll use when you really can take the request — short, confident ownership at work.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 没问题 to accept a task with confidence, often followed by 我来处理. It sounds capable; overusing it before scope is clear creates false commitment. Clarify timing and details first, then say 没问题.

example.zh: 没问题，我来处理这个事情。
example.pinyin: Méi wèntí, wǒ lái chǔlǐ zhège shìqing.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as shōudào. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 收到邮件. Hindari: 收到 only confirms receipt; it does not automatically mean you agree with the content.
words.when: Remember 收到 like the word you’ll use when a work chat, email, file, or instruction has landed and you need a one-word acknowledgment.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers ping 收到 in office chat to mean “got it / noted,” especially for messages and files (收到邮件). It confirms intake, not approval — if you disagree or cannot comply, say so after 收到.

example.en: Got it — I’ll arrive on time.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as qǐngwèn. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 请问一下. Hindari: do not put 请问 after the question; place it at the start.
words.when: Remember 请问 like the word you’ll use when you open a polite ask to someone you do not know well, or when the setting is formal.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers put 请问 (or 请问一下) at the front of a question to soften a request for information. It belongs before the question, not tagged on at the end. Common in meetings, lobbies, and first contacts with colleagues.

example.zh: 请问，这个会议几点开始？
example.pinyin: Qǐngwèn, zhège huìyì jǐ diǎn kāishǐ?
example.en: Excuse me — what time does this meeting start?

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as bù hǎoyìsi. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 不好意思，打扰一下. Hindari: for a serious mistake, add a clear explanation and apology; this phrase alone can feel too light.
words.when: Remember 不好意思 like the word you’ll use when you gently interrupt, ask someone to repeat, or own a small workplace disturbance — not only for big faults.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers open with 不好意思 to soften an interruption or a missed hearing (没听清楚), often with 打扰一下. It signals politeness more than deep guilt. For real errors, follow with what went wrong and a clearer apology.

example.zh: 不好意思，我刚才没听清楚。
example.pinyin: Bù hǎoyìsi, wǒ gāngcái méi tīng qīngchu.
example.en: Sorry — I didn’t catch that just now.

words.en: could I trouble you; please (polite ask)
words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as máfan nǐ. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 麻烦你看一下. Hindari: do not use this as a literal “you’re annoying”; here 麻烦 is a polite request, usually followed by a concrete action.
words.when: Remember 麻烦你 like the word you’ll use when you politely ask someone to do a slightly inconvenient favor — send a file, check something, share an address.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers soften asks with 麻烦你 + a specific verb phrase (看一下, 发给我). In workplace Mandarin it is courtesy, not complaint. Never gloss it as calling the other person troublesome.

example.pinyin: Máfan nǐ bǎ dìzhǐ fā gěi wǒ.
example.en: Could I trouble you to send me the address?

words.en: are you free?; is now a good time?
words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as fāngbiàn ma. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 现在方便吗. Hindari: 方便 asks about availability or ease, not emotional “comfort.”
words.when: Remember 方便吗 like the word you’ll use before a call or a short ask — you give the other person room to refuse or postpone.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers check 你现在方便吗？ before taking someone’s time on the phone or in person. It is about schedule availability, not whether they feel emotionally comfortable. A no is socially acceptable; wait for yes before diving into the question.

example.zh: 你现在方便吗？我想问个问题。
example.pinyin: Nǐ xiànzài fāngbiàn ma? Wǒ xiǎng wèn ge wèntí.
example.en: Are you free now? I’d like to ask a question.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as xīnkǔ le. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 今天辛苦了. Hindari: do not use it as an opener before someone has started working.
words.when: Remember 辛苦了 like the word you’ll use after someone finishes a task or a long workday — appreciation that is extremely common in Chinese workplaces.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers say 辛苦了 (often 今天辛苦了) to thank colleagues after effort, sometimes with 早点休息. Timing matters: it lands after work is done, not as a greeting before the shift starts.

example.en: Thanks for your hard work today — rest early.

notes.title: Choosing among 好的 / 行 / 可以 / 没问题
notes.body: Modul 01 treats these as graded workplace replies, not synonyms. 好的 is the safe neutral acknowledgment for instructions and agreements (chat or face-to-face). 行 is a short casual yes when a proposal already fits you; with a new boss, prefer 好的. 可以 is more neutral than 行 and often marks permission or that a plan is possible (可以安排) — personal ability is often 能 instead. 没问题 is confident ownership when you truly can deliver; do not say it if timing or details are still unclear.

example.zh: 好的，我下午把文件发给你。
example.pinyin: Hǎo de, wǒ xiàwǔ bǎ wénjiàn fā gěi nǐ.
example.en: Okay — I’ll send you the file this afternoon.

notes.title: 收到 confirms receipt, not agreement
notes.body: In work chat, 收到 (pairing: 收到邮件) means the message, file, or instruction arrived. The book warns that it does not automatically mean you agree with the content — acknowledge first, then accept, push back, or clarify.

example.en: Got it — I’ll arrive on time.

notes.title: Polite openers: 请问 / 不好意思 / 麻烦你
notes.body: 请问 (请问一下) opens a polite or formal question and must come at the start, not after the question. 不好意思 softens an interruption, a repeat request, or a minor disturbance (不好意思，打扰一下); for serious mistakes, add explanation and a clearer apology. 麻烦你 politely asks someone to do a slightly inconvenient concrete action (麻烦你看一下) — it is not “you’re annoying.”

example.pinyin: Máfan nǐ bǎ dìzhǐ fā gěi wǒ.
example.en: Could I trouble you to send me the address?

notes.title: 方便吗 checks availability, not comfort
notes.body: Before calling or taking a short slice of someone’s time, ask 现在方便吗 / 你现在方便吗？ so they can refuse or postpone. Here 方便 is about schedule availability or ease of talking — not emotional “comfort.”

example.zh: 你现在方便吗？我想问个问题。
example.pinyin: Nǐ xiànzài fāngbiàn ma? Wǒ xiǎng wèn ge wèntí.
example.en: Are you free now? I’d like to ask a question.

notes.title: 辛苦了 comes after the work
notes.body: 辛苦了 (今天辛苦了) is a very common Chinese workplace thank-you after someone finishes a task or a tiring day, often with 早点休息. The book’s Hindari: do not use it as an opener before work has started.

example.en: Thanks for your hard work today — rest early.

notes.title: Latihan 90 detik (book exercise)
notes.body: Book drill on p.8: pick three entries from this module — 好的, 收到, and 方便吗 — and build one work or daily story that uses all three. Record without reading the PDF, then check whether your timing and decisions came out clearly. No model Chinese dialogue is printed for this drill; do not invent one as book text.

example.zh: 好的 / 收到 / 方便吗
example.en: Target trio for the 90-second practice (instruction only; no sample story in the book).
